title: fix(autoround): pre-seed fp_ref from IntermediatesCache to skip collect_reference
body:
## Summary

AutoRound's \`collect_reference\` runs a full FP16 forward pass over all
calibration inputs at the start of every \`quantize_block\` call to obtain
reference outputs for SignSGD optimization. With \`propagate_error=False\`
(the default), \`SequentialPipeline\` already holds the identical tensors
in \`IntermediatesCache[k+1]\` — \`collect_reference\` is a duplicate that
exhausts CPU RAM for large N on big models (~39 GB/rank at N=8192,
seq=6144, hidden=3072, 8-GPU DDP).

Fix: before \`sequential_epoch_end\` fires, extract the next subgraph's
hidden states from \`IntermediatesCache\` and deliver them to the modifier
via \`set_fp_ref_outputs()\`. \`apply_autoround\` passes them to
\`quantize_block(reference_output=...)\`, skipping \`collect_reference\`
entirely. Falls back to the existing path when absent (last subgraph, or
\`propagate_error=True\`).

Two files changed in llm-compressor, ~45 lines.

> **Companion PR to intel/auto-round merged** — intel/auto-round#2289 (merged 2026-09-04)
> added \`reference_output\` to \`CompressionOrchestrator.quantize_block\`.
> The parameter is guarded with \`inspect.signature\` so existing installs
> (auto-round <=0.15.0, the current PyPI max) silently fall back to \`collect_reference\`
> as before. The optimized path activates automatically once auto-round 0.16.0 is
> released on PyPI; a follow-up PR will bump the \`setup.py\` pin to \`>=0.16.0\` at
> that point.

Also adds a docstring note to \`AutoRoundModifier.enable_torch_compile\` recommending
\`False\` for multi-GPU DDP with large models (per-rank compilation time can exceed the
NCCL watchdog timeout).

Closes #3129
Depends on: #3055 (merged)

## Test Plan

- Ran N=8192, seq=6144, iters=200, \`enable_torch_compile=False\` on 122B MoE
  (8 × H20 140 GB, 8-GPU DDP):
  - v1-2 model: before fix → CPU RAM OOM + NCCL watchdog timeout at layer 44;
    after fix → ✅ 49/49 blocks completed, ~10 h, peak system RAM ~310 GB
  - v1-3 model: after fix → ✅ all 8 ranks SUCCESS, 31291 s (~8h42m)
- \`make quality\` passes
- See linked Issue for quantization quality evaluation results

title: Sequential Pipeline Offloading
body:
It's good to start small. This is just the offloading changes, without the moe linearization/repacking updates. 

### Sequential Pipeline Offloading
Removed the use of the offload context in the sequential pipeline. Onload/offload is manually managed now. 

Onloading is done as
```python
offload_kwargs = onload_modules(subgraph_modules)
```
`subgraph_modules` is a hash as dict[str, module] where the key is the module's name. 
`offload kwargs` are in the form dict[str, dict]. Values are in the form returned by `get_cache_init_kwargs`

Offloading done as:
```python
offload_modules(subgraph_modules, dict(offload_kwargs))
```

We do this so that we can swap out modules from the `subgraph_modules` when doing eager linearization/repacking easily. These operations create new module objects that need to be bound to the model. In addition, the old ones need to have all references deleted so that they can be freed, regulating our memory usage. 

Onload/Offload functions under `src/llmcompressor/pipelines/sequential/offloading.py`.

title: [REAP] Refactor pruning report to per-expert saliency scores
body:
## Summary

Refactors the report produced by `REAPPruningModifier` and adds a report-only mode.

- **Report data is now `list[list[float]]` serialized with `pickle`.** One inner list of per-expert saliency scores per MoE layer, ordered by layer. Replaces the previous JSON map of retained expert indices per layer.
- **The report no longer stores which experts were retained.** Instead it stores the `saliency` score of each expert (`tracker.mean_saliency`), recorded on the source rank after the distributed reduction.
- **New top-level attribute `prune: bool = Field(default=True)`.** When `prune=False`, the model weights and config are never modified — pruning is skipped in both `on_sequential_epoch_end` and `on_finalize` — while saliency is still computed via the calibration hooks so a report can be written.
- **Validation:** at least one of `report_path` or `prune` must be set (otherwise REAP would do nothing). `report_path` must now end with `.pkl` (was `.json`).

## Testing

- `test_base.py`: extended `test_reap_validation` (`.pkl` extension + `report_path`/`prune` mutual requirement) and added `test_reap_report_only_does_not_modify_model`, verifying the model is untouched under `prune=False` and the pickled report has the expected `list[list[float]]` shape.
- `test_ddp.py`: loads the report via `pickle`, uses `.pkl` paths, and compares per-layer saliency with `torch.testing.assert_close`.
- `make style` / `make quality` pass; REAP unit tests pass.

title: [REAP] Skip support for GPT-OSS
Sequential Pipeline Prefetching Threads
body:
Part 2 -- implementing prefetching.

Successor to https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/3208

With the onload/offload out of a context, we can do two important things for performance. 

1. Offloading should not be blocking: Once we are done with a subgraph, we can begin the next subgraph iteration while the current subgraph offloads in the background. 
2. Prefetching the next subgraph: During calibration + propagation, we can start onloading the next subgraph. 

Change some oneshot args:

`sequential_prefetch` --> `sequential_activation_prefetch`
This is more clear about what it does -- prefetching next activations. This is also required so that it doesn't get confused with the other new flag. 
Added `sequential_module_prefetch`
This one enables prefetching of the next subgraph's modules. 

Maybe these should just be combined to enable everything?


Turning these on speeds things up, at the cost of more memory usage.

title: Sequential Offloading, Linearization + Repacking
body:
Changes to linearization, repacking, sequential pipeline offloading. 

## Implementation

### Sequential Pipeline Offloading
Removed the use of the offload context in the sequential pipeline. Onload/offload is manually managed now. 

Onloading is done as
```python
offload_kwargs = onload(subgraph_modules)
```
`subgraph_modules` is a hash as dict[str, module] where the key is the module's name. 
`offload kwargs` are in the form dict[str, dict]. Values are in the form returned by `get_cache_init_kwargs`

Offloading done as:
```python
offload(offload_modules, dict(offload_kwargs))
```

We do this so that we can swap out modules from the `subgraph_modules` when doing eager linearization/repacking easily. These operations create new module objects that need to be bound to the model. In addition, the old ones need to have all references deleted so that they can be freed, regulating our memory usage. 

Onload/Offload functions under `src/llmcompressor/pipelines/sequential/offloading.py`. 


### Linearization and Repacking

We add flags `moe_eager_linearize_repack` (Linearize and/or repack each subgraph during calibration onload if `True`, linearize and/or repack before/after the whole model is calibrated for `False) and `repack_moe` (Whether or not to pack experts to 3d). 

Before calibration, we trace the whole model and build a hash for fast lookup for all moe modules -- packed or not packed. This is stored on the model as `model._moe_lookup`. Generated by `get_moe_linear_status`. 

This lookup is important because using model.get_submodules(name) traverses the whole model which is a taxing operation for large models. 

From here, we have functions as follows:
`linearize_moe_model`
`linearize_moe_subgraph`
`linearize_moe_layer`

and their corresponding repacking/reverse counterparts
`repack_moe_model`
`repack_moe_subgraph`
`repack_moe_layer`

The `*_model` functions are used with `sequential_linearize_repack=False`. They iterate over moe layers, onloading/offloading each layer individually (If you can't fit an entire moe layer on gpu at once, you're out of luck). 

Some things to note:

Weird hard-to-read code such as:
```python
    linearized = [
        (moe_lookup[module], module)
        for module in subgraph_set
        if module in moe_lookup and isinstance(module, LinearExperts2D)
    ]

    for i in tqdm.tqdm(range(len(linearized)), desc="Repacking experts in subgraph"):
        repack_moe_layer(model, linearized[i][0], linearized[i][1])
```

In the case that we are linearizing/repacking and the resulting new module is a new object, we want to free the old object. This can only be done when the python object is garbage collected. So here we make sure that the old module's reference is deleted by the end of its iteration. This is also why we need:

```python
        gc.collect()
        if torch.accelerator.is_available():
            torch.accelerator.empty_cache()
```

At the end of a sequential pipeline subgraph iteration, we don't generate enough objects to force automatic garbage collection (at least for the tests I've run). The cache release might have a solution but I haven't been able to dig it up yet. Without that part it seems that we constantly have allocated but unused gpu memory.

title: Add a narrow GLM MTP save path
body: This shows the simpler alternative to #3118: upstream Transformers' `MtpModel` attaches GLM MTP layers so the normal `QuantizationModifier` calibrates the backbone and MTP together in one pass, while a focused `save_pretrained` hook serializes copied, BF16-dequantized, or NVFP4 MTP weights ([validated model](https://huggingface.co/soyrsoyr/glm-4.5-Air-NVFP4-MTP)).

title: MoE Linearization and Offloading Changes
body:
Move moe linearization and repacking (same operation but reversed) to be handled by the pipeline. Currently linearization is handled at load time, requiring an onload + offload operation. Repacking is not currently used in any pipelines, and is also added to pipelines. 

## Implementation

We add a `disable_offloading_controlled` context which takes in a subgraph, onloads everything, then offloads at the end. Note that we have to wrap the modules in `OnloadWrapper`'s in order to keep track of onloading/offloading. The modules themselves also get a pointer to their `OnloadWrapper`. This is because when we linearize or repack, we actually generate fully new modules, so we need to maintain a way to track the most recent module. 
 * Considering having the `OnloadWrapper` attached to the model, so that it's replace function handles in swapping modules and deleting references from any hashes *

We add flags `sequential_linearize_repack` (Linearize and/or repack each subgraph during calibration onload if `True`, linearize and/or repack before/after the whole model is calibrated for `False) and `repack_moe` (Whether or not to pack experts to 3d). 

Before calibration, we trace the whole model and build a hash for fast lookup for all moe modules -- packed or not packed. This is stored on the model as `model._moe_lookup`. Generated by `get_moe_linear_status`. 

This lookup is important because using model.get_submodules(name) traverses the whole model which is a taxing operation for large models. 

From here, we have functions as follows:
`linearize_moe_model`
`linearize_moe_subgraph`
`linearize_moe_layer`

and their corresponding repacking/reverse counterparts
`repack_moe_model`
`repack_moe_subgraph`
`repack_moe_layer`

The `*_model` functions are used with `sequential_linearize_repack=False`. They iterate over moe layers, onloading/offloading each layer individually (If you can't fit an entire moe layer on gpu at once, you're out of luck). The `*_subgraph` functions are assumed to be under a `disable_offloading_controlled` context. 

Some things to note:

Weird hard-to-read code such as:
```python
    linearized = [
        (moe_lookup[module], module)
        for module in subgraph_set
        if module in moe_lookup and isinstance(module, LinearExperts2D)
    ]

    for i in tqdm.tqdm(range(len(linearized)), desc="Repacking experts in subgraph"):
        repack_moe_layer(model, linearized[i][0], linearized[i][1])
```

Under these new contexts, since we want to constantly free up memory, we need to be careful with how we put out references. Iterating naively `for name, module in linearized` makes it such that linearized maintains a reference to the module. In the case that we are linearizing/repacking and the resulting new module is a new object, we want to free the old object. To my knowledge this can only be done when the python object is garbage collected. So here we make sure that the old module's reference is deleted by the end of its iteration. This is also why we need:

```python
        gc.collect()
        if torch.accelerator.is_available():
            torch.accelerator.empty_cache()
```

At the end of the new load context. We don't generate enough objects to force automatic garbage collection (at least for the tests I've run). The cache release might have a solution but I haven't been able to dig it up yet. Without that part it seems that we constantly have allocated but unused gpu memory. 



Added tests. 

Using example under examples/sequential_linearization/gemma4_example.py:
```python

model_id = "google/gemma-4-26B-A4B"
with load_context():
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_id,
        device_map="auto_offload",  # fit as much as possible on cpu, rest goes on disk
        #max_memory={0: 0, "cpu": 16e9},  # remove this line to use as much cpu as possible
        offload_folder="./offload_folder",  # folder to store offloaded weights
    )
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

...


oneshot(
    model=model,
    dataset=DATASET_ID,
    dataset_config_name=DATASET_SUBSET,
    splits=f"train[:{NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES}]",
    recipe=recipe,
    max_seq_length=MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH,
    num_calibration_samples=NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES,
    sequential_linearize_repack=True,
    repack_moe_layers=True,
)

```

# Time for one shot
Main: 175s
New (Sequential linearization): 119s
New (Upfront linearization): 139s

Since the timing doesn't include load, the main branch branch takes additional time for load-time linearization. 

The timings for the old version are highly dependent on the offload memory allocation `max_memory`. If we limit gpu memory as well we can throttle to nearly infinite time. This version is always faster. 

Can use the offload examples to compare old/new performance

title: [Datatsets] Respect num_calibration_samples when loading calibration data
body:
Previously num_calibration_samples was only applied in the DataLoader sampler, after the entire split had been loaded and tokenized. And with no split specified, all splits were loaded as a DatasetDict and a downstream fallback only knew how to pick a "train" split (breaking ultrachat_200k, which has train_sft/test_sft).

- Add TextGenerationDataset.DEFAULT_SPLIT so each dataset resolves its own default split (ultrachat_200k -> train_sft, flickr30k/peoples_speech -> test, custom -> None); base defaults to "train".
- Collapse a multi-split DatasetDict to a single split before processing.
- Trim to num_calibration_samples before the preprocess/tokenize maps so we don't tokenize samples the sampler would only discard.
- Simplify get_processed_dataset's split handling accordingly.

## Calibration data resolution

| Config | Calibration samples come from |
|---|---|
| `splits` + `num_calibration_samples` | `num` samples **from your split** (shuffled → seed-42 subset; unshuffled → the `num` longest in the split) |
| `splits` only | Same, with the implicit default 512 (split < 512 → whole split + warning) |
| `num_calibration_samples` only | 512 from the class `DEFAULT_SPLIT` (`train`, `train_sft`, `test`, …) |
| neither | `DEFAULT_SPLIT`, trimmed to the default 512 |
| `num_calibration_samples=None` | The whole split (no trimming) |
| `concatenate_data=True` | `num` *packed chunks* selected by the sampler (packing may yield fewer) |

The trim is only applied where it doesn't change the sampled set: it is skipped when `concatenate_data=True` (the sampler must count packed chunks, not rows) and when `shuffle_calibration_samples=False` (`LengthAwareSampler` must see the whole split to pick the longest sequences). The multi-split `DatasetDict` fallback picks the lexicographically first split so the choice is deterministic.

title: Fix recipe merge with pre-numbered stages
body:
SUMMARY:

Preserve existing numbered recipe stages when merging a duplicate unnumbered stage. Previously, an existing `<name>_stage_0` entry could be overwritten while `<name>_stage` was renamed, silently dropping that stage's modifiers.

The merge now selects the next available suffix for both the original unnumbered stage and the incoming stage while preserving the existing stage order. Regression tests cover the normal duplicate case and the collision with an existing numbered stage, including key order.

title: Add MoNe pruning support
body:
## Summary

The PR adds [MoNE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.00390) (Mixture of Experts and Novices) pruning support for MoE models. MoNe has an original codebase https://github.com/zxgx/mode-pd from paper authors, we rely on it in our integration and provide a benchmark comparison. 

The MoNe method is close to [REAP](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13999v1) but instead of removing redundant experts it replaces them with constant vectors that are their unbiased estimators. In our extensive experiments MoNE outperforms REAP on a wide range of benchmarks.

The implementation is tested on `allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924` following the paper experiments and achieves comparable average score across 9 benchmarks from the paper. We also add support for a larger model, particularly minimax-m2.5.

Details:

- Adds a `MoNEPruningModifier` that collects calibration statistics, ranks experts, preserves the top experts, and replaces pruned experts with approximate constant experts.
- Adds generic MoNE model support/registry utilities plus MiniMax-M2 support including native FP8 expert handling.
- Wires MoNE into the pruning modifier registry, pipeline registry, and model loading path for saved MoNE checkpoints.
- Adds checkpoint export validation and fixes cross-device embedding re-tying during save.
- Adds unit coverage for MoNE modifier behavior, MiniMax MoNE layout/export logic, linearized loading, pipeline registry integration, and save utilities.

## Testing

- `pytest tests/llmcompressor/modifiers/pruning/mone/test_base.py tests/llmcompressor/modeling/test_minimax_mone.py tests/llmcompressor/modeling/test_linearize.py::test_olmoe_uses_olmoe_experts_for_linearized_loading -q`

## Benchmarking

OLMoE model scores using original codebase (mode-pd) vs llm-compressor implementation. The scores on individual benchmarks fluctuate a bit but the average across 9 tasks is comparable. 


| Benchmark     | Metric   | mode-pd | llm-compressor | Delta   |
|---------------|----------|--------:|---------------:|--------:|
| ARC-Challenge | acc_norm | 0.4266  | 0.4454         | +0.0188 |
| ARC-Easy      | acc_norm | 0.6465  | 0.7256         | +0.0791 |
| BoolQ         | acc      | 0.6703  | 0.6388         | -0.0315 |
| COPA          | acc      | 0.8600  | 0.8500         | -0.0100 |
| MMLU          | acc      | 0.4029  | 0.3864         | -0.0165 |
| OpenBookQA    | acc_norm | 0.4080  | 0.4080         | +0.0000 |
| PIQA          | acc_norm | 0.7786  | 0.7813         | +0.0027 |
| RTE           | acc      | 0.6462  | 0.6859         | +0.0397 |
| Winogrande    | acc      | 0.6740  | 0.6598         | -0.0142 |
| **Average**   | **mean** | **0.6126** | **0.6201** | **+0.0076** |


## Example command

Run 25% pruning of OlMoE model using zyda2 dataset and 100 calibration steps.

```
from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.modifiers.pruning.mone import MoNEPruningModifier

recipe = MoNEPruningModifier(
    preserve_n_experts=48,      # OLMoE has 64 experts/layer; prune 25%
    ranking_metric="fusion",
    ranking_scope="layer",
    fusion_io_weight=0.5,
    stats_device="cpu",
)

oneshot(
    model="allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125",
    recipe=recipe,
    dataset="Zyphra/Zyda-2",
    dataset_config_name="sample-100BT",
    splits="train[:512]",
    text_column="text",
    concatenate_data=True,
    max_seq_length=4096,
    num_calibration_samples=100,
    shuffle_calibration_samples=False,
    batch_size=1,
    moe_calibrate_all_experts=False,
    pipeline="basic",
    precision="bfloat16",
    save_compressed=False,
    output_dir="./OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-mone-pruned-48",
)
```

title: docs: model-size guidance for scheme selection, language alignment for calibration data
body:
Two documentation gaps I ran into while quantizing Thai models, each backed by paired measurements.

## 1. `choosing-scheme.md` — model size, not just GPU

The scheme table answers *what can my GPU run*. It does not answer *what can my model absorb*, and that turned out to matter more than hardware for us. Same recipe (NVFP4 W4A4 via `QuantizationModifier`), same 512-sample calibration set, same machine, paired per-item against each model's own BF16 source with exact McNemar:

| Model size | Outcome |
|---|---|
| ~30B | multiple-choice recovery within noise (−0.5 pt, n.s.) |
| ~7B | −2.4 pt knowledge (p=0.02), **−10.2 pt instruction following** (p=0.0009) |

Re-running the same 7B as **W4A16** recovered both (−0.7 and −3.7 pt, neither significant) at the same footprint and speed — hence the added rule of thumb to prefer weight-only below ~10B.

The two halves of W4A4 also fail on different task types, which the two arms isolate cleanly: dropping activation quantization fixed instruction following and knowledge, but **mathematical reasoning was unchanged (−5.4 vs −5.6 pt, both significant)** — that damage comes from the 4-bit weights and weight-only does not rescue it.

## 2. `choosing-dataset.md` — language alignment

"Domain alignment" covers general/instruct/code, and all four suggested datasets are English. There is currently no guidance that calibration data language matters, even though calibration is what sets the activation scales. Added a short subsection: use a mixed set (we used 50/50 target-language/English, 512 samples), a snippet for building one, and a note to evaluate in the target language too.

## Framing

These are one lab's numbers on one model family (Thai-capable Qwen2/Qwen3 derivatives, NVIDIA GB10). I wrote both sections as a starting prior with an explicit "validate on your own workload" caveat rather than as universal rules — happy to soften or cut anything that reads as over-claiming. All runs were pre-registered before measurement and the artifacts are public: https://github.com/spped2000/thaillm-nvfp4-dgx-spark

---

*Disclosure: prepared with assistance from Claude (Anthropic). Every figure quoted comes from paired runs on the hardware described.*

title: Add native FP8 expert support to REAP
body:
## Summary:

Currently REAP can't work with fp8 checkpoints because `LinearExperts2D` assumes a checkpoint packs experts as a list of `nn.linear` instances which is true for a lot of models but experts in FP8 checkpoints (at least some of what I saw) are packed all together into a fused container `FP8Experts` so `LinearExperts2D` can't iterate them. This PR fixes the problem.

The only way to use fp8 checkpoints with REAP now is to dequantize chpt in the beginning and run calibration with bf/fp16 weights. This also saved pruned model in bf/fp16 rather than in original fp8 which is ambigious. 

Adds REAP support for packed native FP8 MoE experts, including activation-norm collection and structural pruning while preserving FP8 weights and scales. Updates router and correction-bias pruning and adds coverage for native FP8 expert detection, calibration, and pruning.

## Test plan
Validated with minimax-m2.5 model and 38 REAP tests plus Ruff checks

title: Avoid CUDA indexing failures in iMatrix grid search updates
body:
## Summary

Replace boolean-indexed in-place updates in the iMatrix grid search with shape-validated torch.where selections.

## The change:

- validates that all update tensors and the boolean mask match best_error.shape
- avoids the CUDA advanced-indexing path used by the masked assignments
- preserves the existing no-improvement and patience behavior

## Problem

The current update path can fail during CUDA quantization runs:

python
best_error[improved] = err[improved]
best_min[improved] = shrink_min[improved]
best_max[improved] = shrink_max[improved]


The following failures were observed with GPTQ, NVFP4, and the imatrix_mse observer:

- Gemma 4 E2B: inconsistent selection sizes when the same boolean mask was used on both sides of an assignment
- Gemma 4 E4B: CUDA IndexKernel.cu out-of-bounds device assertions

The exact lower-level cause has not been confirmed, so this change does not assume a specific PyTorch defect. The added shape validation did not trigger during successful patched GPU runs.

## Validation

The development environment used to prepare this change is CPU-only.

CPU validation:

- pytest -q tests/llmcompressor/observers/test_imatrix.py
  - 34 passed
- ruff check
  - passed
- ruff format --check
  - passed
- git diff --check
  - passed
- added a CPU regression test for explicit grid-search shape validation

GPU validation was performed separately using GPTQModifier with NVFP4 imatrix_mse, 1,024 calibration samples, max_seq_length=8192, FP8 static KV-cache calibration, and the basic calibration pipeline for Gemma 4 E models:

- Gemma 4 E2B failed repeatedly before the change and completed on the first run after the change
- Gemma 4 E4B hit CUDA IndexKernel.cu assertions before the change and completed on the first run after the change
- the shape validation did not trigger in either successful run
- quantization and compressed-model saving completed successfully

The same patched environment was used to produce the Gemma 4 QAT NVFP4 collection covering 31B, 26B-A4B, 12B, E4B, and E2B:

https://huggingface.co/collections/yasu-oh/gemma-4-qat-nvfp4

## Trade-off

torch.where materializes full output tensors, so it may use slightly more temporary memory and memory bandwidth than masked in-place assignment.

title: Let AWQ mappings absorb scales into a sliced projection
body:
SUMMARY:

`AWQMapping.smooth_layer` is a single module name, and `_apply_smoothing` folds `1/s`
into that one module's weight. That covers every architecture in the registry today,
because in all of them the balance layers' input is produced by one module (a norm, or
a preceding projection).

It cannot express an AdaLN-modulated block. There the balance layers see

```
norm(x) * (1 + scale) + shift
```

and `scale` / `shift` are slices of one shared projection's output, not modules of
their own. Concretely, in MiniMax-H3's diffusion transformer
(`MiniMaxH3Transformer3DModel`, [diffusers#14355](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/pull/14355)):

```python
shift_msa, scale_msa, gate_msa, shift_mlp, scale_mlp, gate_mlp = self.adaln_proj(temb)
norm_hidden_states = self.norm1(hidden_states) * (
    1.0 + scale_msa.index_select(0, adaln_indices)
) + shift_msa.index_select(0, adaln_indices)
```

There is no module whose weight can absorb `1/s`, so AWQ has nothing to fold into and
these models fall back to `default_mappings`, which do not match.

The absorption does exist, and it is exact:

```
y / s = (norm(x) / s) * (1 + scale) + (shift / s)
```

`norm(x)/s` comes from dividing the norm's weight, and `shift/s` from dividing the rows
of the shared projection that emit the `shift` chunk. `scale` is left alone: it multiplies
elementwise, and the `1 +` term is already handled by the norm weight, so scaling `scale`
as well would double-apply the correction.

This PR adds the smallest thing that can express that:

* `SlicedSmoothTarget(layer, chunk_index, num_chunks, repeat)` names a contiguous row
  slice of another projection's output, in the layout produced by
  `view(-1, num_chunks * hidden)` followed by `chunk(num_chunks, -1)`, tiled `repeat`
  times.
* `AWQMapping.extra_smooth_targets` — an optional list of them, defaulting to empty.
* `absorb_sliced_scales()` applies `1/s` to those rows, weight and bias.
* Mappings for `MiniMaxH3Transformer3DModel`.

I deliberately did **not** widen `smooth_layer`'s type to a union. That would ripple
through `match_modules_set`, `ResolvedMapping`, `_check_layers_are_compatible` and every
registered architecture for no benefit, since the primary smooth layer stays a single
module in this case too. The extra targets are resolved the way
`activation_hook_target` already is, by dotted path, with one difference documented in
the dataclass: they resolve against the module holding `smooth_layer`, not against the
balance layers' ancestor. In an AdaLN block the balance layers sit under `attn` / `ff`
while the shared projection is a sibling of the norm, so resolving against the ancestor
would not find it.

Two things left out on purpose:

* **No `ff.net.0.proj -> ff.net.2` mapping for MiniMax-H3.** That projection is a fused
  SwiGLU, and the existing Linear-smooth branch folds `1/s` into the *last*
  out_features, which here are the gate half. The block output is not linear in the
  gate, so that fold would not be equivalence preserving. Smoothing the up half needs a
  sliced target on the smooth side, which is a separate change; the same gap applies to
  any fused-SwiGLU architecture, not just this one.
* **No diffusion calibration path.** `oneshot` feeds tokenized text, while a DiT takes
  `(hidden_states, temb, adaln_indices, rotary_emb, attention_mask)` that only a real
  sampling run produces. So the mapping this PR registers is not reachable end to end
  from llm-compressor today. I would rather land the mapping mechanism separately from
  the data pipeline, but if you would prefer this to wait until a diffusion calibration
  source exists, say so and I will hold it.

TEST PLAN:

New `tests/llmcompressor/modifiers/transform/awq/test_sliced_smooth.py`, six unit tests
on a synthetic AdaLN block, so nothing here depends on diffusers or on a downloaded
checkpoint:

```
$ pytest tests/llmcompressor/modifiers/transform/awq/ -v -m unit
...
test_sliced_smooth.py::test_absorb_sliced_scales_preserves_output PASSED                  [ 89%]
test_sliced_smooth.py::test_absorbing_the_scale_chunk_is_not_equivalent PASSED            [ 91%]
test_sliced_smooth.py::test_absorb_sliced_scales_only_touches_its_own_chunk PASSED        [ 93%]
test_sliced_smooth.py::test_absorb_sliced_scales_rejects_shape_mismatch PASSED            [ 95%]
test_sliced_smooth.py::test_extra_smooth_targets_resolve_against_the_smooth_layer_parent PASSED [ 97%]
test_sliced_smooth.py::test_minimax_h3_mappings_are_registered PASSED                     [100%]

================ 46 passed, 3 deselected, 14 warnings in 3.34s =================
```

That run covers the whole `transform/awq` directory, so the 40 pre-existing tests in
`test_base.py` and `test_dynamic_mappings.py` are in it and still pass: the new dataclass
field is optional and defaults to empty, so no registered architecture changes behaviour.
Environment: torch 2.13.0+cu130, transformers 5.14.1, compressed-tensors
0.17.2.a20260731, CPU only, no GPU needed.

The load-bearing one is `test_absorb_sliced_scales_preserves_output`: fold `1/s` into the
norm weight and the shift rows, scale the balance layer's input columns by `s`, and the
block's output must be unchanged. In float64 it matches to `rtol=atol=1e-12`.

`test_absorbing_the_scale_chunk_is_not_equivalent` is the control. It does the same thing
but folds into the `scale` chunk instead of `shift`, and asserts the output *changes*.
Without it the first test would pass for the wrong reason, since a no-op would also
"preserve" the output.

One caveat on the usual "does the test fail without the patch" check: for a new API it
fails only with `ImportError`, which proves nothing. That control test is the real guard,
which is why I wrote it.

I also ran the derivation against the real module rather than only the synthetic one.
Building `MiniMaxH3TransformerBlock` from diffusers' `minimax-h3` branch, hidden 64,
float64, and applying the same fold:

```
max abs diff : 2.220e-16
max rel diff : 6.876e-17
control (wrong fold) rel diff: 1.752e-02
```

Checks on the changed files:

```
$ ruff check src/llmcompressor/modifiers/transform/awq/ tests/llmcompressor/modifiers/transform/awq/test_sliced_smooth.py
All checks passed!
```

`ruff format --check` reports one pre-existing reformat in `base.py` (an `assert` at
line ~789) and one in `test_base.py`, neither of which this PR touches; my local ruff is
0.15.18 and evidently differs from the pinned one, so I left both alone rather than add
unrelated churn.

Context: I hit this quantizing MiniMax-H3's 33B joint video/audio DiT to fit on 2x24GB.
`adaln_proj` is 13.0B of the 33.1B parameters there, which is also why keeping it out of
the quantized set matters: the diffusers docstring notes that a rounding applied before
its silu biases every block's modulation identically at every sampling step, so the error
accumulates coherently along the denoising trajectory.

@brian-dellabetta, since you built the mapping mechanism this extends in #2526 and #2451,
and @kylesayrs as a second pair of eyes on the `_apply_smoothing` change. Happy to reshape
the API if you would rather express this differently, or to hold it until a diffusion
calibration source lands.

title: Fix DDP race condition on HF cached_files
body:
SUMMARY:

Fixes #2984.

Ranks loading an **already-downloaded** checkpoint fail with `does not appear to have a file named <shard>` for shards that are present on disk.

`huggingface_hub` rewrites `refs/<revision>` on every `snapshot_download` where the caller passes a symbolic revision, which is what transformers does. The write is a non-atomic truncate-then-write, and it is unconditional, so it runs even when the cache is fully populated and nothing needs fetching:

```python
if revision != commit_hash:                 # _snapshot_download.py
    with open(ref_path, "w") as f:
        f.write(commit_hash)
```

`try_to_load_from_cache` reads that ref with a plain `open`. A rank landing inside the window reads an empty string, fails the `revision not in cached_shas` check, and reports the shard missing. With N ranks each rewriting the ref while the others resolve, spurious missing shards are reliable.

**Fix:** resolve the symbolic revision to a commit hash before loading. `snapshot_download` only touches the ref when `revision != commit_hash`, so loading by hash skips the write entirely. The revision is resolved once and broadcast, so ranks cannot pin different commits if the branch moves between resolutions.

Entered last in `load_context`'s `ExitStack` so it is the outermost patch and the inner contexts resolve against the pinned commit. All 11 DDP examples already go through `load_context`, so no example changes were needed.

Note this is a downstream mitigation. The real fix belongs in `huggingface_hub`, whose `file_download.py` already writes this ref atomically via `_cache_commit_hash_for_specific_revision`; `_snapshot_download` keeps a second inline writer that did not get the same hardening in huggingface_hub#4306. Still present on their `main`. I intend to open that PR too.

Known limitations, happy to address any of them:

- Only covers callers that go through `load_context`.
- If the revision cannot be resolved (offline, gated, no network) it warns and loads unpinned rather than failing, so the race returns in that case.
- Adds one hub API call per load on rank zero, even for a fully cached model.

TEST PLAN:

`tests/llmcompressor/utils/test_dev.py`, 11 cases, mock-based and GPU-free: no-op when single-rank or uninitialized, rank zero resolving and the load using the commit, peers taking the broadcast value without querying the hub, symbolic branches being replaced, skipping when the revision is already a hash / the path is a local dir / the stub is missing, unresolvable revisions loading unpinned, `from_pretrained` restored on exit, and the `ExitStack` ordering.

```
$ pytest tests/llmcompressor/utils/test_dev.py -v
11 passed
```

Reproduction of the underlying race, against a warm cache with no downloads in the measured window, 96 shards, 4 writer and 4 reader processes (script in #2984):

| revision passed | spurious misses | resolution passes |
|---|---|---|
| `"main"` | **7946** | 7033 |
| commit sha | **0** | 7294 |

End-to-end over 2 gloo ranks, recording what revision actually reaches `huggingface_hub`:

```
with the fix:     ['d1abfb7465f27fd86fccb14bcb42e9145ba55d4c']  pinned: True   (both ranks)
without the fix:  ['None', 'main']                              pinned: False  (both ranks)
```

title: [GPTQ] Avoid implicit CUDA sync when logging calibration sample count
body:
## Summary

`GPTQModifier.compress_module_list` formatted the per-module `num_samples`
CUDA scalar tensor directly for a debug log:

```python
logger.info(f"Quantizing {name} using {int(num_samples)} samples")
```

`int(num_samples)` calls `Tensor.item()`, which forces an implicit
`cudaStreamSynchronize` on **every** Linear being quantized. Two problems:

1. **Hang (the filed bug):** under multi-rank DDP with sharded/divergent
   module sets across ranks (e.g. decoupled MoE experts), this sync directly
   follows a `dist.reduce` on the NCCL stream and can block indefinitely
   waiting on a kernel that is no longer pending from NCCL's perspective.
2. **Wasted syncs:** even in the happy path it is a synchronous host stall per
   Linear — tens of thousands of unnecessary `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls on
   a large MoE calibration run, purely to format a log message.

## Change

Materialize the sample count on the host once, explicitly, before logging:

```python
if isinstance(num_samples, torch.Tensor):
    num_samples = int(num_samples.detach().cpu().item())
logger.info(f"Quantizing {name} using {num_samples} samples")
```

The averaged-hessian division is untouched — it still divides by the
on-device tensor via `self._num_samples.pop(module)`, so quantization
numerics are unchanged.

## Scope

This addresses the **log-path host sync** identified in #2736 (the issue's
option (b)). The deeper NCCL-event registration in `wait_for_comms`
(option (a)) requires a multi-rank environment to reproduce and verify and is
left as a follow-up.

## Testing

- `ruff check src/llmcompressor/modifiers/gptq/base.py` passes.
- Logic change is behavior-preserving for the log (same integer value) and
  does not touch the quantization math. No local GPU/multi-rank environment
  was available to reproduce the original hang.

Fixes #2736

title: Add log_sequential_error option for layerwise SQNR-based error reporting
body:
## Purpose

Reports the Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (SQNR) between each sequential subgraph's pre- and post compression outputs during oneshot calibration, using the largest output tensor as a proxy for the subgraph's main activation.

SQNR (not KL divergence — the issue was updated after discussion, since KL divergence is for comparing probability distributions, whereas here we're comparing differences in raw activation values) is computed directly from accumulated signal/noise power sums:

    SQNR = 10 * log10(signal_power_sum / noise_power_sum)

Enabling this option forces `propagate_error=True` since both unquantized and quantized outputs are needed for comparison.

## Changes

* Add `log_sequential_error` option to `DatasetArguments` and the `oneshot()` entrypoint (default `False`)
* New module `pipelines/sequential/error_logging.py` holds all SQNR logic, keeping `pipeline.py`'s original loop structure intact:
  * `cache_pre_compression_output()` — selects a subgraph's main activation (largest tensor in its output dict) and stashes it in the shared `IntermediatesCache` under a reserved key, so it inherits the pipeline's existing CPU/disk offloading instead of accumulating in a raw Python list/dict (avoids OOM on large calibration datasets)
  * `accumulate_batch_power()` — compares the cached pre-compression tensor against the post-compression output for a batch, returning `(signal_power_sum, noise_power_sum)`, then frees the cached tensor
  * `compute_sqnr()` — computes one SQNR value from accumulated power sums across all batches in a subgraph, rather than averaging a per-batch SQNR (dB is a logarithmic ratio, so arithmetic-averaging it is not meaningful, and would let a single zero-noise batch skew the whole subgraph's result to `inf`); mirrors the accumulate-then-normalize pattern already used by `AWQModifier._compute_loss`
* In `SequentialPipeline`, force `propagate_error=True` when `log_sequential_error` is enabled, taking precedence over the existing `AutoRoundModifier` override, and log the per-subgraph SQNR via a `SequentialPipeline`-named logger patch (matching `IndependentPipeline`'s existing convention)
* Add unit tests (`test_log_sequential_error.py`) covering both the enabled and disabled paths using the `nm-testing/tinysmokellama-3.2` smoke model

## Test Plan

```python
from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.modifiers.gptq import GPTQModifier

recipe = GPTQModifier(targets="Linear", scheme="W4A16", ignore=["lm_head"])

oneshot(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",
    dataset="open_platypus",
    splits="train[:64]",
    max_seq_length=256,
    num_calibration_samples=64,
    pipeline="sequential",
    log_sequential_error=True,            # For #3154
    recipe=recipe,
)

title: [Discussion] StreamingPipeline: meta-device async subgraph prefetch for dense + MoE
body:
## Summary

This is a **discussion Draft PR** for the streaming subgraph prefetch described in Issue #3132, extended to MoE models. The `pipeline.py` file is a `NotImplementedError` placeholder — the goal is to share the `checkpoint.py` implementation and benchmark results for review before writing the full `StreamingPipeline.__call__`.

Benchmark discussion (3 comments): https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues/3132#issuecomment-5776372775

## What's in this PR

`src/llmcompressor/pipelines/streaming/`

- **`checkpoint.py`** — Core utilities for the meta-device pipeline:
  - `CheckpointMap`: lightweight param_fqn → (shard_file, key, dtype, shape) index built from safetensors headers only (~7ms for 0.6B, <1s for 72B; no weights read at construction)
  - `stage_modules`: disk→CPU staging grouped by shard (background-thread safe; safetensors releases GIL during I/O)
  - `commit_staged_async`: H2D transfer queued on a dedicated CUDA stream — the sole addition over PR #3111's blocking `commit_staged`
  - `release_modules`: replace GPU params with meta tensors in <1ms (no disk write)
  - `MetaSubgraphPrefetcher`: wraps `stage_modules` in a background thread

- **`pipeline.py`** — `StreamingPipeline(CalibrationPipeline)` skeleton (`NotImplementedError` placeholder)

- **`__init__.py`** — Public exports

## Three-layer pipeline

```
Disk bg:    [read sg_N+1 ──────────]
H2D stream:                   [DMA sg_N+1 ──]
GPU:        [compute sg_N          ]  [wait≈0ms]  [compute sg_N+1 ────]
```

`inject_wait_s ≈ 0ms` validated across all 48 configurations tested (dense 27B/72B × 4 configs; MoE 30B × 6; MoE 235B × 6).

## Benchmark highlights

| Model | Best speedup | Key driver |
|-------|-------------|-----------|
| MoE 30B-A3B (N=16–128) | **15.1×** | `load_s` elimination (430–670s → 0.2s) |
| MoE 235B-A22B | **1.74×** | `load_s` elimination (2400–3200s → 26s) |
| Dense 72B (N=128, sl=2048) | **1.52×** | GPTQ compute dominates; sync overhead amortized |

A 235B model (~447 GB bf16) can be fully GPTQ-calibrated end-to-end on a **single L20 (48 GB)** — no model sharding, no multi-GPU coordination. This mirrors vLLM's deployment-time weight loading pattern applied to calibration.

## Related PRs / Dependencies

- **[PR #3111](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/3111)** (@Isotr0py) — `StreamingPipeline` base architecture: `CheckpointMap`, `SubgraphPrefetcher`, blocking `commit_staged`, `release_modules → meta`. This PR's `commit_staged_async` is the only addition.
- **[PR #3208](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/3208)** (@Roderick-Wu) — `load_quantizable_moe()`: MoE expert linearization at load time. Required for MoE support.
- **[PR #2995](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/2995)** + **[CT PR #811](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/811)** (@kylesayrs) — per-subgraph `allowed_modules` + `leave_decompressed=False`: needed for the full compress-and-release loop.
- **[Issue #3131](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues/3131)** — streaming model saving (`stream_write` step): remaining unimplemented layer.
- **[CT PR #883](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/883)** (@ishrith-gowda) — `disk_load_context()`: grouped shard reads for DiskCache path (complementary).

## Questions for reviewers

1. Is the `commit_staged_async` CUDA stream approach the right abstraction, or should H2D be handled differently in the `StreamingPipeline.__call__` loop?
2. Should `CheckpointMap` live here or in a shared utility module (e.g. alongside `IntermediatesCache` in `pipelines/cache.py`)?
3. Is `release_modules → meta` the right approach for GPU memory recovery, given that quantization scales written during calibration are intentionally preserved?

title: fix(dist): write back broadcast qparams to offload storage on non-src ranks
body:
## Summary

`broadcast_qparams_and_cleanup` calls `dist.broadcast` on module attributes such as `weight_scale`, `weight_zero_point`, and `weight_g_idx`. When these tensors are stored in `CPUCache` (the common case with sequential pipeline `auto_offload`), `getattr(module, name)` returns a **temporary onloaded GPU tensor** — a new allocation each call. `dist.broadcast` modifies that temporary in-place, but the underlying CPU storage is never updated — leaving non-source ranks with stale or uninitialised quantization parameters.

**Trigger conditions:** multi-GPU DDP GPTQ with sequential pipeline and `auto_offload=True`, typically used to parallelize activation collection over large calibration sets. The quantization completes silently with no exception; the corruption only appears when inspecting saved checkpoints.

This PR adds an explicit `update_offload_parameter` writeback for non-source ranks after `_wait_for_comms`, which correctly flushes the broadcast result back to CPUCache storage.

## Changes

- `src/llmcompressor/utils/dist.py`: collect `(module, name, param, broadcast_param)` for non-src-rank entries before issuing async broadcasts; after comms complete, copy back and call `update_offload_parameter` (+40/-2 lines)
- `tests/llmcompressor/utils/test_broadcast_qparams_writeback.py`: unit tests covering non-src writeback, src no-writeback, missing params, and multi-module cases
- `tests/llmcompressor/utils/test_cpucache_temporary_tensor.py` (new): 3 unit tests proving CPUCache returns a new temporary CUDA tensor per `getattr` call and that in-place modification is lost without writeback
- `tests/llmcompressor/utils/test_broadcast_qparams_ddp_integration.py` (new): 2-GPU integration test using real `dist.broadcast` + real CPUCache, demonstrating the bug (Phase A) and fix (Phase B) in a single distributed session

## Empirical validation

Controlled A/B on 8× L20, `Qwen3.5-122B-A10B`, N=5120, seq=6144:

| | with fix | without fix |
|---|---|---|
| rank 0 SCALE_CHECK | ✅ CLEAN (total=37056) | ⚠️ CORRUPTED nan=31924 neg=402 |
| rank 1 SCALE_CHECK | ✅ CLEAN | ⚠️ CORRUPTED nan=840 inf=1 neg=3139 |
| rank 4 SCALE_CHECK | ✅ CLEAN | ⚠️ CORRUPTED nan=3829 neg=3 |
| all 8 ranks | CLEAN | multiple ranks CORRUPTED |

Full details in issue #3119.

Fixes #3119

title: Add QuantizationAwareDistillationModifier for block-wise QAD
body:
## Summary

- Adds `QuantizationAwareDistillationModifier` that performs block-wise quantization-aware distillation in the sequential pipeline
- Captures teacher outputs during calibration forward pass (before any modifier modifies weights), then optimizes student weights via MSE distillation using the standard compressed-tensors quantized forward (implicit STE via weight.data patching)
- Can run standalone (with its own `scheme`/`targets`/`ignore` via `QuantizationMixin`) or compose with GPTQ in a shared sequential pipeline (`pipeline="sequential"`)
- Configurable `master_precision` option (default `"float32"`) for optimizer weight precision to avoid gradient underflow with small learning rates
- Re-observes quantization scales after each epoch to keep them aligned with updated weights

### Key design choices vs #3029

| | This PR | #3029 |
|---|---|---|
| Teacher source | Cached calibration outputs (0 extra memory) | Separate model instance (2x memory) |
| Standalone mode | Yes (via QuantizationMixin) | No (requires GPTQ first) |
| Multi-layer subgraphs | Yes | No (requires 1 per subgraph) |
| Scale re-observation | Every epoch | Never |
| fp32 master weights | Configurable | No |
| Pipeline changes | None | Yes |
| Code size | ~290 lines | ~1300 lines |

## Test plan

- [x] Standalone QAD smoke test (`test_qad_smoke.py`) — Llama 3 8B, W4A16, 32 samples, 2 epochs — passes in ~50s
- [x] GPTQ + QAD composition test (`test_gptq_qad.py`) — shared sequential pipeline — passes in ~6m25s

title: Fix #2984: prevent DDP race on shared HF cache during model loading
body:
## Problem

Every DDP example calls `from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, ...)` on all ranks
immediately after `init_dist()`. The `dist.barrier()` inside `init_dist()`
only synchronizes the process group — it says nothing about the filesystem
or HF cache state. Right after it returns, every rank races into
`from_pretrained` independently, and `transformers`/`huggingface_hub`
internally performs cache checks and downloads for each shard. With N
ranks hitting the same shared `HF_HOME`/`TRANSFORMERS_CACHE` at once
(the typical single-node multi-GPU `torchrun` setup), this can produce
partially-written blobs, reads of a config/index file mid-write, or
corrupted/incomplete cache entries.

I checked the repo for an existing rank-0-downloads-first guard and
didn't find one — no `accelerator.is_main_process`, `PartialState`, or
manual `if rank == 0: download(); barrier()` pattern exists in `src/`
or `examples/`.

## Fix

Adds `prefetch_model_on_rank0()` in `src/llmcompressor/utils/dist.py`.
Rank 0 calls `snapshot_download` to fully populate the shared cache,
then all ranks hit a `dist.barrier()`, so every rank's subsequent
`from_pretrained` call reads from an already-complete local cache
instead of racing to write it. No-op for local paths or non-distributed
runs.

Wired into two examples as a reference pattern:
- `examples/quantization_w8a8_int8/smoothquant_ddp_example.py`
- `examples/quantization_w4a16/llama3_ddp_example.py`

The same unguarded pattern exists in ~9 other DDP examples in the repo
(AWQ, AutoRound, imatrix, sequential offloading, MoE examples). Happy
to open a follow-up PR to wire the helper into those as well once this
approach is confirmed — wanted to keep this first PR small and reviewable.

I also checked `copy_python_files_from_model_cache` (which calls
`hf_hub_download` for `config.json`), since it looked similarly
unguarded — but it's already wrapped in `if is_source_process():` in
`compressed_tensors_utils.py`, so no fix needed there.

## Testing

- `tests/llmcompressor/observers/test_fusion_handler.py` (exercises
  `llmcompressor.utils.dist`): 28 passed
- `tests/llmcompressor/transformers/smoothquant/test_smoothquant_distributed.py -m unit`: 3 passed
- Collection-only pass (no errors) on the DDP/multi-GPU integration
  tests: `test_smoothquant_distributed.py`, `test_compression_ddp.py`,
  `test_quantization_ddp.py`, `test_dist_disk_offload.py`,
  `test_distributed.py`, `test_example_scripts.py`

I don't have multi-GPU hardware available locally, so I wasn't able to
run the actual `@requires_gpu(2)` / `@pytest.mark.multi_gpu` integration
tests. Would appreciate a maintainer running those in CI to confirm.

Fixes #2984

title: [Feature] Add block-wise QAD with shared data and weight re-observation
body:
## Summary

Adds block-wise local quantization-aware distillation after a preceding weight quantization method. During the existing calibration forward, QAD hooks cache a decoder block's inputs and unquantized outputs. At `sequential_epoch_end`, the preceding method prepares quantization, QAD reconstructs the cached outputs, and the existing pipeline propagates the final quantized outputs.

- Share one calibration dataset and dataloader. No changes to the pipeline, public lifecycle, Modifier base class, or oneshot entrypoint.
- Compose RTN (`QuantizationModifier`) or `GPTQModifier` followed by `QADModifier`. The tested AWQ composition is `AWQModifier` → `QuantizationModifier` → `QADModifier`; AWQ's transform still needs a weight quantization modifier. Other methods use the same lifecycle contract; QAD does not inspect GPTQ-specific state or quantizer class names.
- Follow the weight re-observation schedule in #3051: before training, after every epoch, and before final materialization. Observe all modules before updating any qparams to preserve fused NVFP4 global scales.
- Retain masked MSE, FP32 optimizer master weights for FP16/BF16 execution, dynamic FP16 loss scaling, gradient accumulation/clipping, deterministic validation, early stopping, and best-checkpoint restoration. Restore matching weight qparams with the best weights. `reobserve_weights=False` retains a fixed-scale option.
- Use one complete target module per subgraph, local teacher targets, single-process calibration, and `propagate_error=True`. Ignore the output LM head. Full teacher streams, separate QAD datasets, and arbitrary multi-target graph reconstruction are outside this version.
- Keep `LayerwiseQADModifier` as an alias. Usage and quantizer composition requirements are documented in `examples/qad/`.

## Validation

- CPU: QAD tests plus `tests/llmcompressor/core/test_session_functions.py` — 39 passed, 4 accelerator cases skipped. Regression cases cover long-sequence FP16 gradient underflow, unscaling before clipping, complete/partial accumulation groups, overflow retries, and persistent nonfinite-gradient failure. The experiment training/export/reload entrypoint also passes a tiny CPU check with source/input provenance validation.
- H200 on the corrected source: 41 passed, 2 CPU-only cases skipped. Covers all QAD tests, including FP16 long-sequence gradients, overflow recovery, exact teacher-input propagation, RTN/GPTQ/AWQ+RTN composition with NVFP4A16/W4A16, and RTN/GPTQ FP16 NVFP4 save/reload/generation.
- Changed Python files pass Ruff lint/format and CUDA portability checks. Full `make quality` reaches two existing import-order errors in unchanged sparsity tests.
- An additional check on main `8ada4c40` with compressed-tensors `698967f` encounters a `weight_global_scale` Tensor/Parameter error in the dependency's post-save offload conversion; the same error reproduces with GPTQ alone. The existing experiment environment passes save/reload.
- Paired Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct experiments use shared UltraChat budgets 512/1024/2048, evaluation seeds 1234/2345/3456, five benchmarks, and WikiText-2 PPL (context 2048, stride 512). All six checkpoints passed quantization, export and reload validation; 18/18 full evaluations are verified, including all nine complete GPTQ/QAD budget/seed pairs. Each condition has one trained checkpoint (training seed 42); the three seeds are evaluation repeats.
- The three GPTQ-only checkpoints and nine baseline evaluations are reused. Comparing archived runtime sources confirms that only QAD training code changed. Model/data revisions, calibration token IDs, hyperparameters and the evaluator are pinned. Accepted corrected QAD evaluations pass the same complete protocol, sample and paired-input checks.

## Corrected 8B results — 512, 1024 and 2048 samples

**All six checkpoints and 18 full evaluations are verified.** These results use the corrected FP16 loss-scaling implementation in `cdf35548` and replace the earlier, pre-correction QAD measurements. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, NVFP4A16, shared nested UltraChat calibration data, training seed 42. Entries are mean ± sample standard deviation over evaluation seeds 1234/2345/3456, using one saved checkpoint per condition.

title: HIGGS: ILP-based mixed-precision quantization
body:
## Overview

HIGGS is a technique from [this](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.17525) paper which can be used to determine the theory-based optimal mixed-precision quantization configuration to use to quantize a model given a constraint on the average quantization bitwidth the user wants. Note in the paper there are 2 methods for calculating how sensitive each layer is to quantization, this PR only implements the heuristic method.

HIGGS has 2 phases, it first collects a bunch of MSE data and layer location information to estimate layer sensitivity to quantization, it then converts this information to an ILP and then uses PuLP to solve the ILP and generate an optimal quantization config. This config can then be passed into oneshot or model_free_ptq to actually quantize the model.

All the above functionality lives in the HiggsMSECollectorConverter which is supported by the get_higgs_config entrypoint since our converter architecture makes a number of assumptions about the converter actually applying quantization to the model. In the future we could get rid of get_higgs_config. 

## Results

| Target Bits | NVFP4A16 Layers | FP8_DYNAMIC Layers | word_perplexity |
|-------------|-----------------|---------------------|-----------------|
| 4.0 | 224 | 0 | 9.9381 |
| 4.5 | 124 | 100 | 9.8493 |
| 5.0 | 92 | 132 | 9.7695 |
| 5.5 | 75 | 149 | 9.7209 |
| 6.0 | 61 | 163 | 9.6805 |
| 6.5 | 46 | 178 | 9.6384 |
| 7.0 | 30 | 194 | 9.5992 |
| 7.5 | 15 | 209 | 9.5674 |
| 8.0 | 0 | 224 | 9.4934 |
| 16.0 (base) | 0 | 0 | 9.4236 |

As you can see, a straightforward bitwidth sweep from 4-8 yields consistently monotonic  PPL improvement as the target bitwidth grows. While such a growth is not strictly guaranteed given that after all HIGGS doesn't take into account activation quantization accuracy and only has a local estimate of weight quantization accuracy, it performs extremely well (especially for such a fast technique). These results were generated using the higgs_nvfp4a16_fp8_model_free.py example. Note we use the nvfp4_expanded_mse observer to get a better than RTN quantized model both for error estimates for HIGGS and the final quantization.

As mentioned above though HIGGS can compose with oneshot for quantization schemes that require calibration:

| Example | Schemes | Method | HIGGS Time | Quant Time | PPL |
|---------|---------|--------|------------|------------|-----|
| `higgs_nvfp4_fp8_qmod` | NVFP4 + FP8_DYNAMIC | QuantizationModifier | 8.05s | 1:21 | 9.7502 |
| `higgs_nvfp4_fp8_gptq` | NVFP4 + FP8_DYNAMIC | GPTQModifier | 7.64s | 3:24 | 9.7486 |

As you can see we're able to apply GPTQ or just use a normal QuantizationModifier after HIGGS, you can do things like AWQ as well though that may invalidate the HIGGS scheme's theoretical optimality.

Also note the speed of this HIGGS implementation, since we use a model_free method to collect MSE values without writing anything, we are able to do this incredibly quickly, for all the models i've tested HIGGS takes up a minority of the time compared to the actual application of quantization. This massively outperforms other designs in terms of speed even if you were to pre-quantize the model to each candidate scheme. The process of reading N different model weights into memory in order to calculate MSE is much slower than just calculating it all from scratch, even though some work is duplicated due to weights needing to be quantized both to calculate MSE and to save the final quantized model.

these results were generated using the /home/HDCharles/repos/llm-compressor/examples/quantization_higgs/higgs_nvfp4_fp8_gptq.py example.

## Files

llmcompressor/entrypoints/higgs/base.py - contains MSE collection code and general orchestation (HiggsMSECollectorConverter and get_higgs_config

llmcompressor/entrypoints/higgs/ilp_solver.py - our ILP setup/solver

llmcompressor/entrypoints/higgs/utils.py - all helpers/utils includes the code that calculates the heuristic alpha (layer sensitivity based on location in model)

title: Report recipe ignore entries that matched nothing at save time
body:
SUMMARY:

`save_pretrained_wrapper()` writes two descriptions of the same run: the resolved quantization config, via `compressor.update_config()`, and the recipe itself, via `update_and_save_recipe()`. Nothing checks that the recipe's entries correspond to anything in the model at the moment they are written.

An `ignore` entry that matches no module is the case where those two descriptions can drift apart quietly. Nothing about it is incorrect today — the configuration is applied exactly as written, and the checkpoint is a faithful record of what was resolved — but the author's intent and the resolved configuration have diverged, and the checkpoint that ships carries the recipe saying one thing and the config saying another. A stale entry is easy to produce: a module renamed upstream, a regex written against an older layer naming, a recipe copied between checkpoints or between model families.

Export is the last point at which that is still cheap to see. After the write, the entry is in the saved recipe and the resolved configuration is in `config.json`, and reconciling them is the consumer's problem.

This adds `warn_on_unmatched_ignore_entries()` and calls it from `save_pretrained_wrapper()` before anything is written. `modifiers/quantization/group_size_validation.py` is the existing precedent for validating a recipe against the model it will be applied to; this is the same kind of check at a different moment, and unlike that one it only warns.

**On the cost of this, stated plainly:** it puts a check on the user-facing export path, so it can surface a new warning on checkpoints that build cleanly today. That is a real cost and I would rather name it than have you find it. What it does not do: it does not raise, does not change what is written, does not change any resolved configuration, and does not gate the save. It changes what a producer *says*, not what it produces.

**Scope — only `ignore` is checked.** Unmatched `targets` already surface: `apply_quantization_config` calls `match_named_modules(..., warn_on_fail=True)`, which warns per unmatched target at initialize. `ignore` in that same signature is consumed by `is_match()` and has no equivalent, so an entry matching nothing is silent everywhere. Checking targets here too would duplicate a warning that already exists, so it does not.

Two smaller decisions:

- **Gated on `is_source_process()`**, so a distributed save reports each entry once rather than once per rank.
- **Only module names and classes are examined**, no parameters, so this does not onload an offloaded model. An entry also stops being tested once it has matched, so the work is bounded by the entries that will be reported.

TEST PLAN:

New `tests/llmcompressor/transformers/compression/test_recipe_validation.py`:

- unit: an entry matching nothing is reported; entries matching by name, by regex and by module class are not; only the unmatched subset is reported out of a mixed list; entries are attributed per modifier; an empty recipe reports nothing; the warning names both the entry and the modifier and does not mention entries that matched.
- integration: saving a model whose recipe carries one non-matching `ignore` entry emits the warning exactly once, **and the checkpoint is otherwise unchanged** — reloaded state dict compared key-by-key and tensor-by-tensor against the model. Saving with `ignore` entries that all match emits no such warning.

Verified the integration test fails without the call site in `save_pretrained_wrapper()` and passes with it, so the wiring is covered and not just the helper.

Locally, on a CPU-only host: `make quality` clean. `pytest tests/llmcompressor/transformers/compression` → 27 passed, 29 skipped. `pytest tests/llmcompressor --ignore tests/llmcompressor/transformers` → 465 passed, 75 skipped, 0 failed. (`tests/llmcompressor/modifiers/quantization/test_handling_shared_embeddings.py` calls `get_accelerator_type()` at module scope and cannot be collected without an accelerator; that is unrelated to this change and was excluded from the run.)

---

*Disclosure: this change was written with AI assistance. I have read and understand every line, and I am responsible for it.*

title: Fix activation caching for dataclasses that validate their fields
body:
Caching activations containing a strict dataclass currently reconstructs the object with `type(value)(**wrapped_fields)`. Its constructor validates each `IntermediateValue` wrapper against the original field type and rejects it. The concrete Mistral object is `transformers.models.mistral3.configuration_mistral3.Mistral3Config` used by Mistral-Small-3.2; its nested text config is another configuration object.

The fix shallow-copies the dataclass and writes the transient wrapped fields with `object.__setattr__`, then uses the same mechanism to restore fields on load. This bypasses constructor and assignment validation without mutating the original object.

Reproduced on 2026-09-14 with Transformers 5.14.1 and huggingface_hub 1.31.0, without model weights or PyTorch:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields
from transformers import Mistral3Config

@dataclass
class IntermediateValue:
    value: object
    device: object = None

config = Mistral3Config()
wrapped = {f.name: IntermediateValue(getattr(config, f.name))
           for f in fields(config)}
type(config)(**wrapped)
```

This raises `StrictDataclassFieldValidationError` for `transformers_version`: `IntermediateValue(value=None, device=None)` is neither `str` nor `None`. The exact `_replace_fields` helper from this PR successfully wrapped and restored that same real config, with `restored.to_dict() == config.to_dict()` and the original left unchanged.

The existing regression test exercises a validating dataclass through the actual cache. Its original PR receipt reports the full cache file at 17 passed. The 2026-09-14 revision adds the missing DCO sign-off only; its code tree is byte-identical to cf2ead8127ddbc7ef8855f51e30d156e86c2b769. Fresh hosted checks and maintainer approval remain required.

title: [Bugfix] Load preprocessing functions from file paths in import_from_path
body:
## Purpose

Fixes #3193

`import_from_path` documents three accepted forms, and
`TextGenerationDataset.preprocessing_func` repeats the first one in its own comment:

```
"/path/to/file.py:func_or_class_name"
"/path/to/file:focn"
"path.to.file:focn"
```

Only the third worked, so pointing `preprocessing_func` at a file — the documented way to
supply a custom calibration preprocessing function — always failed.

`importlib.import_module` takes dotted module names, not file system paths, so the
function rewrote the path first:

```python
path = original_path.split(".py")[0]
path = re.sub(r"/+", ".", path)
```

- A leading `/` becomes a leading `.`, so an absolute path becomes a relative import and
  raises `TypeError`, which the surrounding `except ImportError` does not catch — the
  intended `Cannot find module with path ...` message never appears.
- `split(".py")` cuts at the first `.py` substring anywhere rather than at the extension,
  truncating a dotted path at any package starting with `py`.
  `llmcompressor.pytorch.utils.helpers` becomes `llmcompressor`, which imports
  successfully, so the wrong module is searched and the user sees a misleading
  `AttributeError`.
- `path.split(":")` also raises `too many values to unpack` on `C:/models/prep.py:preprocess`.

## Changes

- load the module from the file when the path points at one, falling back to
  `importlib.import_module` for dotted names
- split the object name with `rsplit(":", 1)`
- `import_from_path` had no test coverage; add tests for the three documented forms and
  both error paths

Behaviour for the form that already worked (a plain dotted module name) is unchanged, as
are the `ImportError` / `AttributeError` messages.

## Test Plan

```
pytest tests/llmcompressor/utils/test_helpers.py -k import_from_path
pytest tests/llmcompressor/utils/
make quality
```

## Test Result

- `-k import_from_path`: 5 passed. 4 of the 5 fail on `main` and pass with this change
  (the fifth covers the missing-module path, which already worked).
- `tests/llmcompressor/utils/`: 5 failed, 15 passed — identical 5 failures on `main`
  (5 failed, 10 passed there); they are `test_disable_lm_head` and
  `test_untie_word_embeddings_gpu`, which need a model download and CUDA respectively and
  cannot run on my machine. No new failures.
- `make quality`: clean.

title: feat: preserve and optionally quantize MTP layers in oneshot
body:
## Summary

Current Transformers loading omits MTP layers in these supported checkpoint layouts. This PR processes them during `oneshot()` saving, both `output_dir` and deferred `model.save_pretrained()`, and writes the MTP shard, safetensors index, and runtime quantization metadata alongside the compressed backbone.

- `mtp_quant_scheme=None` (default) reproduces a compatible source MTP format through the compressed-tensors converter. A preset or `QuantizationScheme` applies data-free quantization.
- `mtp_dequantize=True` saves BF16 when no scheme is requested and permits BF16 fallback if conversion cannot be applied. It does not override an explicit target scheme; backbone and MTP dequantization are independent.
- Supported layouts: Qwen3.5/Qwen3.8-27B dense, GLM-5.3 Flash/DSA, and NemotronH. Qwen3.5 MoE supports dense MTP preservation and BF16 conversion only.
- Source layouts, shard headers, and native FP8 scales are validated; fused projections are quantized together. Missing shards, source dequantization errors, and checkpoint write failures remain fatal.

This path is data-free. Calibration-dependent MTP quantization (static FP8, NVFP4 W4A4, GPTQ/AWQ) and nonuniform MTP schemes are out of scope. See the saving guide for API examples and supported formats.

## Test plan

- Focused tests cover small Qwen load/save fixtures and a pinned GLM-5.3 Flash MTP checkpoint, including immediate/deferred save, source-format reproduction, BF16 conversion, data-free quantization, index/config integrity, and failure cases. `make quality` and `git diff --check` pass.
- Full-model vLLM speculative-decoding smoke tests passed for Qwen3.8-27B and GLM-5.3 Flash/DSA on B200s. See the [validation table](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/3118#issuecomment-5669821394) and [pinned checkpoints and runtime evidence](https://huggingface.co/datasets/soyrsoyr/pr3118-mtp-e2e-validation). These runs were on identified earlier PR commits, not a serving rerun of the current head or quality/performance benchmarks.

## Compatibility and known limits

- Native block-FP8 MTP dequantization requires compressed-tensors 0.18.1: `FP8BlockDequantizer.validate()` in 0.18.0 returns `None`. The release dependency still pins 0.18.0 and needs updating before merge.
- Twelve native-FP8 Qwen test cases fail during Transformers 5.16.1 model loading, before `oneshot()`. They pass locally with 5.17.0; the current release range allows 5.16.1 but excludes 5.17.0. Resolve the supported range or this load path before claiming it.
- Nemotron MXFP4 serving remains blocked by a vLLM MoE scale-loading issue.

Broader MTP representations can be revisited as upstream Transformers support is integrated.

title: Add layerwise decompression and compression to sequential pipeline
body:
## Summary
- Add `layerwise_decompression` and `layerwise_compression` flags to `DatasetArguments` for the sequential pipeline
- When `layerwise_decompression=True`, each subgraph's compressed modules are decompressed (stripping all quantization metadata), then quantization config, observers, and hooks are re-applied per-layer before calibration
- When `layerwise_compression=True`, quantized modules are compressed back after calibration and error propagation to reduce peak memory
- `QuantizationModifier` conditionally skips global setup (`on_initialize`, `on_calibration_start`, `on_calibration_end`) when layerwise mode is active, deferring to per-layer setup via `start_layerwise_calibration`
- Fix `freeze_module_quantization` to preserve `COMPRESSED` status (not overwrite with `FROZEN`)

## Companion PR
- compressed-tensors: https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/811 (`leave_decompressed` parameter + `allowed_modules` support in `apply_quantization_config`)

- [ ] Test layerwise decompression with a pre-compressed FP8 model
- [ ] Test layerwise compression reduces peak memory vs without

title: Implement streaming quantization pipeline
body:
SUMMARY:
"please provide a brief summary"

- This PR implement streaming quantization pipeline to avoid offload/dispatch overheads for efficient quantization on extremely large models
- Firstly, we initialize model on meta device, than prefetch and h2d weights for each layer on demand similar to distributed layerwise offload (DLO): https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-17-distributed-layerwise-offload
- Not DLO yet, will implement it in a followup PR after this PR merge


TEST PLAN:
"please outline how the changes were tested"
## Setup

- Hardware: 1 node, 4x NVIDIA GB300 (284 GiB each), 956 GiB RAM; checkpoints on
  a shared network filesystem.
- Recipe (same as `examples/quantizing_moe/glm5_example.py`): FP8_BLOCK for
  attention, NVFP4 for MLP, `lm_head` and first layers ignored.
- Calibration: 8 samples, batch size 4, seq len 1024, identical pre-tokenized
  data for both pipelines. Saving was not timed.

## Example code

Baseline and streaming differ only in model loading and the `pipeline` argument;
the recipe is identical.

<details>
<summary>Baseline (auto_offload + sequential)</summary>

```python
import torch
from compressed_tensors.offload import init_dist
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.utils import load_context

init_dist()  # requires torchrun
model_id = "zai-org/GLM-5.2"
with load_context():
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_id,
        device_map="auto_offload",
        max_memory={"cpu": "500GiB"},
        offload_folder="offload_folder",
    )
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

oneshot(
    model=model,
    dataset="perfectblend",
    batch_size=4,
    recipe=recipe,
    num_calibration_samples=512,
)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Streaming (meta skeleton + checkpoint-referenced layers)</summary>

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.utils import load_context

model_id = "zai-org/GLM-5.2"
with load_context(meta=True):
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="meta")
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

oneshot(
    model=model,
    dataset="perfectblend",
    batch_size=4,
    recipe=recipe,
    pipeline="streaming",  # default for meta-device models
    num_calibration_samples=512,
)
```
</details>

## Results

### Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (82 GiB bf16, 40 MoE layers x 256 experts, fused 3D expert checkpoint)

Baseline ran with `max_memory={"cpu": "20GiB"}` to force the disk-offload path.

| Phase | baseline (`auto_offload` + `sequential`) | `streaming` | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model load | 128.2 s | 2.1 s | 61x |
| `oneshot` (calibration + layer dispatch) | 328.5 s | 198.5 s | 1.65x |
| **Total (no save)** | **460.0 s** | **207.8 s** | **2.2x** |

### Reduced GLM-5.3-BF16 (12 layers, 176 GiB, per-expert checkpoint, local NVMe)

| Phase | baseline (`auto_offload` + `sequential`) | `streaming` | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model load | 20.4 s | 2.8 s | 7.3x |
| `oneshot` | 146.6 s | 112.0 s | 1.3x |
| **Total (no save)** | **171.7 s** | **118.1 s** | **1.45x** |

title: Pack only weighted modules in distributed oneshot
body:
SUMMARY:
Fixes #3103.

With a `kv_cache_scheme`, an input-activation-only scheme (`weights=None`) is attached directly to the attention containers matched by `is_cached_attention_module` (vllm-project/compressed-tensors#780). Those containers pass `is_module_quantized`, so they land in the quantized-module list that `on_sequential_epoch_end` hands to `greedy_bin_packing`, but they have no `.weight`, and distributed weight calibration crashes with `AttributeError` at the first sequential epoch boundary.

This keeps the quantized-module list intact for `sync_obs_act_stats` / `update_qparams(..., ACTIVATION_OBS)`, which finalize `k_scale`/`v_scale` on those containers, but restricts the weight-calibration bin packing to modules that actually carry a weight tensor. Single-GPU runs are unaffected.

TEST PLAN:
- Added `test_ddp_smoke_rtn_kv_cache` in `tests/llmcompressor/transformers/compression/test_compression_ddp.py`: a 2-rank torchrun run asserting the distributed kv scales are finalized (finite, positive, sane magnitude) and agree with the single-GPU reference.
- On upstream `main`, the distributed run crashes with the reported error:
  ```
  src/llmcompressor/modifiers/quantization/quantization/base.py:100: in on_sequential_epoch_end
      module_list, rank_to_modules, module_to_rank = greedy_bin_packing(
  ...
  AttributeError: 'Qwen3MoeAttention' object has no attribute 'weight'
  ```
- With this fix the same run passes on 2x NVIDIA A40 (`torchrun --nproc_per_node=2`, torch 2.10.0+cu128, transformers 5.16.1, compressed-tensors 0.18.1a20260824):
  ```
